source_purpose.locator: cached PDF page 1; native text slice
source_purpose.quote:
The main aim of this study is to present a technically robust and pragmatic methodology for evaluating
rainwater harvesting potential and identifying suitable sites for RWH and artiﬁcial recharge structures
using Geographic Information System (GIS)-based multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA). Unlike past
studies, this study proposes an approach to prioritize zones/sites for RWH and recharge structures, which
is of great importance for the effective implementation of RWH strategies. The derived themes ‘runoff
coefﬁcient’ and the basic themes of ‘slope’ and ‘drainage density’ were used for mapping rainwater
harvesting potential. Thereafter, suitable zones and sites for feasible RWH and recharge structures were
identiﬁed using suitability criteria and GIS-based Boolean logic.

retained_profile.source_model: West Bengal, India. Three-theme RWH Potential Index preceding separate structure-specific Boolean siting for farm ponds, stream/ground percolation tanks and check dams.
retained_profile.direction: Higher local RWH potential rank at lower micro-watershed drainage density.
retained_profile.unit: km/km², Table 3/PDF3, Fig. 11/PDF13; length divided by micro-watershed area, PDF8.
retained_profile.source_input: ArcHydro drainage from SRTM DEM. Slope and drainage density layers use 90 m SRTM. Density computed from stream length / micro-watershed area and incorporated into a polygon-based WLC index. Local mapped range 0.01–4.86 km/km² (PDF14) describes the input. The 50 m stream-order corridor for installation sites is a different step.
retained_profile.boundaries_and_prose: Strict <0.25 is Very High; the row beginning at 0.25 is High. Adjacent closed-looking printed ranges share 0.50 and 0.75; authors report no exact tie convention there. Other classes, including Very Low, have positive feature weights. Table 3 prospect labels order suitability, whereas Fig. 11/PDF13 and PDF14 describe density magnitude itself in the opposite verbal order. The two scales agree.
retained_profile.lineage: Method section PDF8 cites Jha et al. (2014) for selection of themes. Local weights arise from expert judgments. No source establishes this particular class break as a universal requirement.
retained_profile.evidence_comparison: Corrected current EV already stores all five classes, both sets of weights and use limitation. The inherited scalar numerically matches this study’s first break. Origin of the historical weighted-median calculation has not been reconstructed.

claims.source_review_note: Singh et al. (2017) use stream length per micro-watershed area. Table 3 ranks <0.25, 0.25–0.50, 0.50–0.75, 0.75–1.00 and >1.00 km/km² from very high to very low. Exactly 0.25 starts the second class. Theme weight 0.261 and all five positive feature weights belong to the RWH potential index. Structure siting comes later in a Boolean analysis.
claims.dashboard_reason: Next mapping review. Singh et al., Table 3, rank micro-watersheds for rainwater-harvesting potential. The five drainage-density classes in km/km² are <0.25 (very high), 0.25–0.50 (high), 0.50–0.75 (moderate), 0.75–1.00 (low) and >1.00 (very low). The class starting at 0.25 is high. The normalized theme weight is 0.261. The paper later selects individual structures using separate criteria.

retained_profile.source_model: Ettazarini (2021). Eight-factor AHP model for check-dam site selection in Khenifra province, Morocco, favouring surface-water accumulation.
retained_profile.direction: Higher drainage density receives higher suitability scores for check dams in this model.
retained_profile.unit: km/km², defined in PDF8 as total stream length divided by drainage area. Table 1 omits the unit in its factor label.

source_weight.locator: Table 2 and Eq. 7, PDF7; CR PDF12.

retained_profile.source_input: ASTER-based 30 m DEM and flow-accumulation-derived streams. ArcGIS line density applied with a 500 m stream-length threshold for including streamlines. The 500 m criterion defines the stream network. Density neighborhood/search radius is unresolved in the cited text. Local maximum 1.94 km/km² describes the input.
retained_profile.boundaries_and_prose: Table 1/PDF6, discussion PDF8 and Figure 5B/PDF10 agree on increasing ranking. Middle ranges share 0.4 without a printed tie rule. Lowest category receives 1. Accuracy checks of the combined map against terrain depressions do not validate individual drainage-density breakpoints.
retained_profile.lineage: PDF8 cites Horton (1945) for runoff/infiltration interpretation and Rahmati et al. (2019) for dam-siting preference. Four class scores and 0.07 AHP weight are attributed to Ettazarini’s applied model.
retained_profile.evidence_comparison: Existing EV retains direction. Table 1 class boundaries/scores, scale-dependent network specification and Table 2 criterion weight are surfaced here pending evidence review.

claims.source_review_note: Ettazarini (2021) gives higher drainage density higher check-dam suitability in Morocco. Table 1 scores <0.2, 0.2–0.4, 0.4–0.6 and >0.6 km/km² as 1, 2, 3 and 4. Eq. 7 gives criterion weight 0.07. The 30 m DEM network uses a 500 m minimum stream length. The EV currently records direction only.
claims.dashboard_reason: Next mapping review. Ettazarini mapped check-dam sites. Table 1 assigns increasing scores 1, 2, 3 and 4 to <0.2, 0.2–0.4, 0.4–0.6 and >0.6 km/km². The source uses a 30 m DEM, a 500 m minimum stream length and a drainage-density criterion weight of 0.07. The evidence row captures the direction. The source review also retains the four printed classes.

dashboard_question: Should we hold the shared drainage-density rule that sets 0.25 km/km² as the upper edge of the optimum range, keeping all three quantitative profiles for synthesis by purpose, structure and stream-network definition? Farm-pond and check-dam rankings run in opposite directions. The existing dataset hold is already applied.
